extractor.note: Partial pass over Chapter Two and Chapter Five, where the reduction and the eidetic reduction are thematic.

coverage_note: Covers Chapter Two, 'Science as Egology', and Chapter Five, 'Eidetic Reduction and Archi-Facticity'. Chapters Six, Eight and Nine also carry hits and are not covered.

units.claim: The reduction is distinguished from Cartesian doubt: it neither negates nor doubts, it is definitive and universal, and it encompasses the psyche that Descartes leaves intact.
units.quote: the phenomenological reduction does not operate through doubt: it never involves negation. It is definitive and universal, and it also encompasses the psyche (whereas Descartes leaves the psyche intact as the foundation)

units.claim: The reduction is the pivot and permanent theme of Husserl's enterprise, the pure origin of all meaning and what opens the phenomenological domain.
units.quote: The reduction is the pivot and the permanent theme of Husserl's entire enterprise. It is the pure origin of all meaning and what opens the phenomenological "domain."

units.claim: The reduction is introduced under pressure from a demand for apodicticity that can only be formulated if the field of transcendental experience is already pre-given.
units.quote: This is done under the pressure of the demand for apodicticity, a demand that itself can only be formulated on the presupposition that the field of transcendental experience is already pre-given.

units.claim: What the reduction puts out of play is the thesis of the natural attitude, that the world is a reality in itself.
units.quote: What is "put out of play" by the reduction is the thesis of the natural attitude — the thesis that the world is a reality in itself, the root of all naturalism.

units.claim: Beyond its methodological function the reduction has a historical sense, putting out of play the modern ontology of mathematical-physical nature.
units.quote: The reduction therefore has, beyond its methodological function, a historical sense: it puts out of play the traditional, modern ontology — the ontology of mathematical-physical nature.

units.claim: Running through the flux of lived experiences under the reduction never yields the pure I as itself a lived or original experience.
units.quote: If, under the reduction, we run through the flux of lived experiences, we will never grasp the pure I as a lived or original experience itself.

units.term: the transcendentally absolute produced by the reductions
units.claim: Husserl warns that what the reductions produce as transcendentally absolute is not what is ultimate, but constitutes itself from a primal source that is truly absolute.
units.quote: the transcendentally "absolute" that the reductions have produced is not really what is ultimate; it is something that constitutes itself in a profound and completely peculiar sense of its own, with its primal source in what is ultimately and truly absolute

units.claim: The charge that transcendental analysis merely transfers the empirical de facto ego onto the transcendental is met only by the transcendental analysis becoming eidetic.
units.quote: Indeed — this would be the case if the transcendental analysis did not become an *eidetic* analysis.
